row.basis: Adam’s expulsion and toil
row.note: The commentary links Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis makes the ground cursed and toil the consequence of his disobedience in the same story.

row.basis: bread by sweat
row.note: The commentary recalls hardship following Adam’s exile; Genesis specifies that he eats bread by the sweat of his face, giving that hardship its daily labor.

row.basis: Terah served other gods
row.note: The commentary’s Abraham asks to be kept from idol worship; Joshua says Abraham’s father and ancestors served other gods, locating the danger his prayer names.

row.basis: God took Abraham across the river
row.note: The commentary has Abraham ask God to keep his family from idols; Joshua recounts God taking Abraham from beyond the Euphrates into Canaan, a narrated removal from his idolatrous setting.

row.basis: not in haste or flight; God goes before
row.note: The commentary defines the guide as one who precedes and describes a calm walk rather than a flight; Isaiah joins both details, saying the departing people need not hurry or flee because God goes before them and guards their rear.

row.basis: hind-like feet on high places
row.note: The commentary’s mountain ridge is long yet easier to climb and its mount has light legs; the psalm combines hind-like feet with being set on high places, an image of sure-footed ascent.

row.basis: righteous walk the same paths transgressors fall on
row.note: The commentary says the road may be the same while the traveler’s manner differs; Hosea says the just walk in the Lord’s right ways while transgressors fall in those very ways.

row.basis: God teaches the way one should walk
row.note: The commentary develops guidance as someone going ahead to show a road; the psalm has God instruct and teach the way the addressee should walk, making the guide’s instruction explicit.

row.basis: Wisdom’s counsel refused
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person keeps the reminder at a distance; personified Wisdom says her hearers rejected her counsel and reproof, a concrete scene of refusing admonition.

row.basis: donkey turns aside from the blocked road
row.note: The commentary’s mount is easy to lead and quick to follow; Balaam’s donkey instead leaves the road when it sees the angel blocking the way, and that refusal protects its rider.

row.basis: Balaam’s way is perverse
row.note: The commentary makes the traveler’s conduct, not the road itself, decisive; the angel tells Balaam that his way is perverse, while the donkey’s apparent deviation is the safer response to the blocked path.

row.basis: two gates and roads with different ends
row.note: The commentary sets a shown route beside a steep climb that is not attempted; Jesus describes a broad road entered by a wide gate that leads to destruction, making the traveler’s chosen way consequential.

row.basis: narrow way leading to life
row.note: The commentary’s two high routes and the unattempted ascent invite comparison with Jesus’ narrow way to life, which few find; this adds a sharply difficult route alongside the easy-way image.

row.basis: one side of the afterlife sees the other
row.note: In the commentary’s cited scene a person in bliss looks down and sees his former companion in Hell; Luke has the tormented rich man lift his eyes and see Lazarus with Abraham at a distance, reversing the direction of the postmortem gaze.

row.basis: horse or mule needs bit and bridle
row.note: The commentary’s animal is pliant and follows readily; the psalm warns against an uncomprehending horse or mule that must be controlled with bit and bridle, a pointed contrast between willing guidance and restraint.

row.basis: wicked like windblown chaff
row.note: The commentary’s verse turns pasture into debris; Psalm 1 uses chaff for the wicked, adding an ethical judgment to the image of vegetation reduced to residue.

row.basis: the wicked way perishes
row.note: The commentary distinguishes the person who follows guidance from the one who avoids it; Psalm 1 contrasts the way of the righteous with the way of the wicked that perishes, giving the two responses different ends.

row.basis: a highway on which even a fool will not stray
row.note: The commentary describes being made ready for the easier way; Isaiah’s holy highway is so clearly marked that even a fool will not err on it, a concrete image of an accessible route.

row.basis: the command is not too hard or far away
row.note: The commentary reads the promised easy way as a facilitated course; Deuteronomy says the command is not too difficult or remote, linking divine instruction with practicable action.

row.basis: choose life or death
row.note: The commentary pairs guidance with the traveler’s response and outcome; Moses sets life and death before Israel and tells them to choose life, a direct choice between destinations.

row.basis: the word is near and doable
row.note: The commentary’s easy way is prepared for its addressee; Deuteronomy places the word in mouth and heart, near enough to do, making accessibility an inward as well as traveled route.

row.basis: the shepherd leads in paths of righteousness
row.note: The commentary pictures a guide leading the way; the psalm’s shepherd restores the speaker and leads him in righteous paths, joining care for the traveler to a directed route.

row.basis: a voice behind says, “This is the way”
row.note: The commentary calls the guide one who goes ahead; Isaiah’s traveler hears a voice behind identifying the way to walk, a concrete reversal of the guide’s position while preserving the path instruction.

row.basis: one lifts a fallen companion
row.note: The commentary’s lexical note describes a weak person walking while leaning on two others; Ecclesiastes says one companion raises another who falls, a close support image though not a description of walking gait.

row.basis: walk without growing faint
row.note: The commentary brings together weakness, light legs, and easy travel; Isaiah says those who wait for the Lord walk without fainting, portraying renewed capacity for the journey.

row.basis: riding camels and following the guide
row.note: The commentary’s easy-to-follow animal carries a rider along a route; Rebekah and her attendants ride camels and follow Abraham’s servant, a concrete guided journey on mounts.

row.basis: Rachel sits on the camel saddle
row.note: The commentary describes a wrapped cover placed over a camel’s hump and then ridden; Genesis has Rachel sit on the camel’s saddle, supplying a biblical riding-seat scene, though it uses the saddle to conceal idols.

row.basis: Jacob tells his household to put away foreign gods
row.note: The commentary contrasts keeping counsel away with Abraham asking God to keep him and his sons away from idols; Jacob directs his household to remove its foreign gods and purify itself, a family-level act of separation.

row.basis: foreign gods buried beneath the oak
row.note: The commentary’s Abraham asks for protection from idol worship; Jacob’s household hands over its foreign gods, which Jacob buries beneath the oak, showing the concrete removal that follows his command.

row.basis: Abraham breaks his father’s idols
row.note: The commentary recalls Abraham’s prayer that he and his descendants be kept from idol worship; Genesis Rabbah’s story of the young Abraham breaking the idols in Terah’s shop interprets that separation as an active rejection of his father’s cult.

row.basis: weary and burdened people receive rest
row.note: The commentary reads the promise of ease as relief on a journey; Jesus invites the weary and burdened to come to him and promises rest, giving the ease image a human burden-bearing context.

row.basis: easy yoke and light burden
row.note: The commentary’s mount is readily led and takes the way with light steps; Jesus calls his yoke easy and his burden light, applying ease to the discipline of following him.

row.basis: God promises to be with Moses’ mouth
row.note: The commentary cites Moses asking God to make his task easy; when Moses objects to speaking, God promises to be with his mouth and teach him what to say, a narrative answer that equips him for the mission.

row.basis: possible Arabic s-w-y / Hebrew שוה cognate
row.note: The commentary reports an Arabic family sense of equality alongside “middle”; Isaiah uses the Hebrew root שוה for being equal or compared. The semantic link is specific, but the cognate relationship needs lexical confirmation and does not carry the camel-seat sense.

row.basis: ancient paths, rest, and refusal to walk
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person leaves the reminder beside his route; Jeremiah tells the people to seek the good ancient path and walk in it, but they answer that they will not walk there, joining guidance, a way, and its refusal.

row.basis: prepare a way in the wilderness
row.note: The commentary develops a guide who goes ahead and a route made easy; Isaiah’s voice calls for the Lord’s way to be prepared in the wilderness, an explicit road-making image.

row.basis: mountains lowered and rough ground made level
row.note: The commentary describes a long ridge that is nevertheless easier to climb; Isaiah pictures hills lowered and rough places leveled so a route can be traversed.

row.basis: donkey riders, saddle-related sitting, and walkers on the road
row.note: The commentary brings together a riding cover, the mount, and a person’s route; Deborah’s song groups donkey-riders and walkers on the road with people sitting on a term sometimes understood as saddle-cloths, though that wording is uncertain.

row.basis: the Shunammite’s urgent ride on an ass
row.note: The commentary describes a mount that follows readily and takes light steps; the Shunammite rides an ass and tells her servant not to slacken the pace, a concrete scene of directing a mount along a journey.

row.basis: God chooses a longer route because the people might turn back
row.note: The commentary’s promise makes the way easier for its addressee; Exodus says God avoids the nearer Philistine route lest the people see war and return to Egypt, showing guidance adjusted to the travelers’ weakness.

row.basis: Adam sent from Eden to till the ground
row.note: The commentary connects Adam’s expulsion from the garden with hardship; Genesis explicitly sends him out of Eden to work the ground, joining exile to the labor that follows.

row.basis: guide our feet into the way of peace
row.note: The commentary develops guidance as showing a road and easing the traveler’s way; Zechariah’s prophecy says the dawn from on high will guide people’s feet into the way of peace, directly joining guidance, feet, and route.

row.basis: straight paths for the feet so the lame may be healed
row.note: The commentary pairs a difficult ascent with weak, swaying walking; Hebrews commands straight paths for the feet so the lame limb will be healed rather than injured, joining path preparation to bodily weakness.

row.basis: strengthen weak hands and feeble knees
row.note: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person relying on support; Isaiah tells the hearers to strengthen weak hands and make firm feeble knees, a concrete bodily response to weakness.

row.basis: the lame leap like a deer
row.note: The commentary links a mount’s light legs with a ridge that can be climbed; Isaiah says the lame will leap like a deer, turning impaired gait into agile movement.

row.basis: a lame man is raised by the hand and strengthened
row.note: The commentary recalls a weak person who needs support to walk; Peter takes the man lame from birth by the hand and raises him, and his feet and ankles are strengthened, a concrete healing of unsupported gait.

row.basis: the healed man walks and leaps
row.note: The commentary’s lexical image is a weak, swaying walker; after the healing in Acts, the man enters the temple walking, leaping, and praising God, showing the restored movement that support makes possible.

row.basis: make level paths for your feet
row.note: The commentary’s mountain ridge is long but easier to climb and its route is made accessible; Proverbs urges the traveler to consider the path of his feet and make his ways firm, a practical image of preparing one’s course.

row.basis: human plans, the Lord directs the steps
row.note: The commentary says the road can be the same while the traveler’s conduct differs; Proverbs contrasts a person’s plans with the Lord’s direction of his steps, clarifying the relation between human course and divine guidance.

row.basis: turn away from the evil path
row.note: The commentary says the wretched person steps aside from the reminder; Proverbs commands the traveler to avoid the wicked path, turn from it, and pass on, a useful reversal in which one should leave the road rather than the warning.

row.basis: a man lame from birth is carried to the temple gate
row.note: The commentary’s secondary walking image is a weak person who relies on support; Acts describes a man lame from birth being carried and placed at the temple gate, a specific scene of dependence before his healing.

row.basis: John identifies himself as Isaiah’s wilderness voice
row.note: The commentary develops the guide and the way that is made ready; John applies Isaiah’s road-preparation oracle to his own role as herald, reading the route as preparation of people for the Lord’s coming.

row.basis: Balaam as one who leaves the straight way
row.note: The commentary says a traveler can take a wrong course while the road remains; 2 Peter interprets Balaam as one who leaves the straight way for wrongdoing, giving the Numbers donkey episode an explicit moral reading of straying for gain.

row.basis: take the yoke, learn, and find rest
row.note: The commentary’s easy mount follows its guide and carries its rider along the way; Jesus invites hearers to take his yoke and learn from him, promising rest for their souls, a distinct image of following under an easy discipline.

row.basis: the shepherd strengthens the sick and binds the injured
row.note: The commentary’s guide imagery includes a weak walker who relies on support; God as shepherd says he will bind the injured, strengthen the sick, and seek the lost, joining direction with care for the weak.

row.basis: be swift as a deer and light as an eagle
row.note: The commentary’s lexicon gives a mount that follows quickly and has light legs; Rabbi Judah ben Tema uses deer-swiftness and eagle-lightness as traits for doing the will of Heaven, turning animal agility into an ethical image.

row.basis: life and death are set before a person to choose
row.note: The commentary links guidance with a traveler’s response and outcome; Sirach says life and death are before a person and the choice is given to him, extending the choice-of-way motif into Jewish wisdom teaching.
